blocks.text: Strychnine poisoning causes violent, painful muscle spasms triggered by the slightest noise or touch, while the patient remains conscious. Strychnine does not make neurones fire more. It removes a brake: it blocks inhibitory receptors on spinal motor neurones. Understanding that brake means understanding how synapses excite and inhibit.

blocks.markdown:
A **synapse** is the junction at which one neurone influences another. At a **chemical synapse** the presynaptic terminal releases a **neurotransmitter** into the narrow **synaptic cleft** (about 20-40 nm); it binds receptors on the **postsynaptic** membrane and changes the postsynaptic membrane potential. Transmission is one-way and introduces a short synaptic delay of the order of a millisecond.

The sequence is: (1) an action potential invades the terminal; (2) depolarisation opens **voltage-gated $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ channels**; (3) $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ enters and triggers vesicles, docked by **SNARE proteins**, to fuse with the membrane (exocytosis); (4) transmitter diffuses across the cleft; (5) it binds postsynaptic receptors, opening channels directly or through second messengers; (6) the transmitter is removed (enzymatic breakdown, reuptake, diffusion away) so the signal ends.

blocks.title: Calcium is the trigger
blocks.text: Release depends on presynaptic Ca2+ entry, not directly on the action potential. Release is steeply dependent on Ca2+ concentration in the terminal, so small changes in Ca2+ entry cause large changes in the amount of transmitter released.

blocks.title: Receptor classes
blocks.text: An ionotropic receptor (ligand-gated ion channel) is itself the channel: transmitter binding opens a pore within milliseconds. A metabotropic receptor is a G-protein-coupled receptor: binding activates a G protein and second-messenger cascade that modulates channels or enzymes more slowly (tens of milliseconds to seconds) with amplification and longer-lasting effects.

rows: Receptor and channel in one complex
AMPA receptor for glutamate; nicotinic ACh receptor
GABA-A receptor (Cl- channel); glycine receptor (Cl- channel)
GABA-B receptor (via G protein, opens K+ channels)

blocks.markdown:
The postsynaptic effect is a graded **postsynaptic potential (PSP)**, not an action potential. An **excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP)** depolarises the membrane toward threshold, typically by opening channels permeable to $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{K}^+$ with a reversal potential near 0 mV. An **inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP)** moves $V_m$ away from threshold or holds it near rest; it usually results from opening $\text{Cl}^-$ channels (reversal potential close to the resting potential) or $\text{K}^+$ channels (reversal near $E_K$).

Whether a PSP depolarises or hyperpolarises depends on where $V_m$ lies relative to the **reversal potential** of the channel that opens: current flows so as to push $V_m$ toward that reversal potential.

blocks.title: Classifying a postsynaptic response from its reversal potential
blocks.prompt: A neurone has $V_m = -65$ mV. A transmitter opens (a) a cation channel with reversal potential 0 mV, (b) a Cl- channel with reversal potential -75 mV. Classify each response.

steps.text: Current drives $V_m$ toward the channel's reversal potential. For (a), 0 mV is more positive than -65 mV, so the membrane depolarises.
For (b), -75 mV is more negative than -65 mV, so Cl- entry hyperpolarises the membrane by pulling it toward -75 mV.
Threshold is about -55 mV: (a) moves toward threshold (excitatory) and (b) moves away (inhibitory).

blocks.answer: (a) is an EPSP and (b) is an IPSP. The classification depends on reversal potential relative to the threshold, not on the transmitter's name.

blocks.markdown: A single PSP is small (often 0.5-5 mV) and decays over a few milliseconds, so one input rarely fires the cell. Neurones **integrate** thousands of inputs. **Spatial summation** adds PSPs arriving at different synapses at the same time. **Temporal summation** adds successive PSPs from one synapse that arrive close enough together that the earlier one has not yet decayed. Summation occurs at the **axon initial segment (axon hillock)**, which has the highest density of voltage-gated Na+ channels and so the lowest threshold. If the summed potential reaches threshold an action potential is triggered.

blocks.title: Summation at the axon hillock
blocks.prompt: A neurone at rest at -70 mV has threshold -55 mV. Six simultaneous EPSPs of +3 mV each and three simultaneous IPSPs of -2 mV each arrive. Assuming linear summation, does it fire?

steps.text: Sum: $-70 + 18 - 6 = -58$ mV, which is still more negative than the threshold of -55 mV.

blocks.answer: No. The membrane reaches -58 mV, short of threshold, so no action potential. One more EPSP of +3 mV would take it to -55 mV, at threshold.

items: Chemical synapses are unidirectional because transmitter is released only from the presynaptic terminal and receptors are postsynaptic.
Termination of the signal is as important as release; transmitters are cleared by enzymes, reuptake transporters and diffusion.
Inhibition is not 'absence of excitation': it is an active change that opposes depolarisation.
Metabotropic signalling adds amplification and modulation but is slower.

blocks.title: Link toxins to steps
blocks.text: Many toxins and drugs act at one step of the sequence: blocking Ca2+ channels, cleaving SNARE proteins, blocking receptors, or blocking removal. Name the step first and the clinical effect follows.

points: Transmission sequence: terminal depolarisation, voltage-gated Ca2+ entry, SNARE-mediated vesicle fusion, diffusion, receptor binding, removal.
Ionotropic receptors are fast ligand-gated channels; metabotropic receptors are slower G-protein-coupled receptors with second messengers.
EPSPs depolarise toward threshold; IPSPs hyperpolarise or stabilise, depending on the reversal potential of the channel opened.
Spatial and temporal summation integrate inputs at the axon hillock to decide whether an action potential is generated.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly orders the key events at a chemical synapse?

options.text: Vesicle fusion, Ca2+ entry, terminal depolarisation, receptor binding
Terminal depolarisation, Ca2+ entry, vesicle fusion, receptor binding
Receptor binding, terminal depolarisation, Ca2+ entry, vesicle fusion
Ca2+ entry, receptor binding, vesicle fusion, terminal depolarisation

questions.correctOptionText: Terminal depolarisation, Ca2+ entry, vesicle fusion, receptor binding

distractorRationale.a: Vesicle fusion cannot precede Ca2+ entry, which triggers it.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: depolarisation opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, Ca2+ triggers exocytosis, then transmitter binds.
distractorRationale.c: Receptor binding is the last step, not the first.
distractorRationale.d: Ca2+ entry itself requires prior depolarisation.

questions.explanation: The action potential depolarises the terminal, opening voltage-gated Ca2+ channels. The Ca2+ entry triggers fusion of docked vesicles, and transmitter then diffuses to postsynaptic receptors.

questions.stem: In an experiment on isolated nerve-muscle tissue, the bathing solution is replaced with one containing a high concentration of Mg2+ and almost no Ca2+. Presynaptic action potentials still invade the terminal, but the postsynaptic potential disappears. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Transmitter cannot diffuse across the cleft
Without Ca2+ entry, vesicles do not fuse and no transmitter is released

questions.correctOptionText: Without Ca2+ entry, vesicles do not fuse and no transmitter is released

distractorRationale.a: Receptors are unaffected by the solution change in this scenario.
distractorRationale.b: Diffusion across a 20-40 nm cleft does not depend on extracellular Ca2+.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: Ca2+ entry through voltage-gated channels is the trigger for exocytosis.
distractorRationale.d: The presynaptic spike still invades, so depolarisation occurs.

questions.explanation: The presynaptic spike is intact, so the step that fails lies between depolarisation and transmitter release. Ca2+ entry couples depolarisation to vesicle fusion, and with no extracellular Ca2+ there is nothing to enter.

questions.stem: A receptor produces a postsynaptic response with a delay of several hundred milliseconds, mediated by a G protein and a second messenger. This receptor is best described as:

options.text: Ionotropic, like the nicotinic ACh receptor

distractorRationale.a: Nicotinic receptors are ligand-gated channels acting within milliseconds.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: G-protein coupling with a second messenger defines a metabotropic receptor.
distractorRationale.c: AMPA receptors are fast ligand-gated channels.
distractorRationale.d: A voltage-gated channel responds to membrane potential, not directly to transmitter via G proteins.

questions.explanation: G-protein coupling and second-messenger signalling are the hallmarks of metabotropic receptors, and they explain the long latency and prolonged action. GABA-B is a metabotropic example.

questions.stem: True or false: an ionotropic receptor contains an ion channel within the same protein complex that binds the transmitter.
questions.explanation: Ionotropic receptors are ligand-gated channels: the binding site and the pore are in one complex, so binding opens the pore directly and quickly. Metabotropic receptors in contrast act through G proteins.

questions.stem: Distinguish ionotropic from metabotropic receptors. Give one example of each and state two differences in the time course or consequence of their action.
markingGuide: Ionotropic: ligand-gated ion channel; binding directly opens the pore
Metabotropic: G-protein-coupled receptor acting through second messengers
Valid ionotropic example (AMPA, NMDA, nicotinic ACh, GABA-A, glycine)
Valid metabotropic example (mGluR, GABA-B, muscarinic ACh, beta-adrenergic)
Ionotropic effects are fast and brief; metabotropic are slower and longer lasting
Metabotropic signalling can amplify the signal and modulate channels or gene expression
questions.explanation: Ionotropic receptors couple binding to channel opening within milliseconds, whereas metabotropic receptors act through G proteins and second messengers. This makes metabotropic responses slower, longer lasting and capable of amplification.

questions.stem: A spinal neurone has V_m = -68 mV. Glycine opens Cl- channels whose reversal potential is -80 mV. What is the immediate effect on the membrane, and how is the response classified?

options.text: No change, because glycine is only metabotropic

distractorRationale.a: 0 mV is the reversal of a non-selective cation channel, not this Cl- channel.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: current drives Vm toward the Cl- reversal potential of -80 mV, which is more negative than -68 mV.
distractorRationale.c: The glycine receptor is an ionotropic Cl- channel.
distractorRationale.d: Threshold is not the reversal potential of the opened channel.

questions.explanation: Opening a channel moves V_m toward that channel's reversal potential. Since -80 mV is more negative than -68 mV the membrane hyperpolarises, moving away from threshold: an IPSP. This is why blocking glycine receptors removes inhibition from motor neurones.

questions.stem: A neurone at rest at -68 mV receives eight simultaneous EPSPs of +3 mV each and two simultaneous IPSPs of -2 mV each. Assuming linear summation, what is the membrane potential in mV at the axon hillock?
questions.explanation: Sum the changes: 8 x (+3) = +24 mV and 2 x (-2) = -4 mV, a net +20 mV. Then -68 + 20 = -48 mV, which is above a typical threshold of about -55 mV, so this neurone would fire an action potential.

questions.stem: A single presynaptic neurone fires five action potentials within 10 ms. Each produces an EPSP of 2 mV that has not fully decayed when the next arrives, so the postsynaptic potential builds up. What is this called?

distractorRationale.a: Spatial summation needs inputs from different synapses at the same time, not one neurone firing repeatedly.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: successive PSPs from one synapse overlap in time.
distractorRationale.c: Lateral inhibition is a different circuit property.

questions.explanation: Temporal summation is the addition of PSPs from the same input that arrive in rapid succession before the previous one decays. Spatial summation would involve multiple different inputs active together.

questions.stem: A toxin enters motor nerve terminals and cleaves SNARE proteins. Which step of synaptic transmission is directly disrupted?

options.text: Binding of transmitter to postsynaptic receptors
Fusion of synaptic vesicles with the presynaptic membrane
Generation of the presynaptic action potential

questions.correctOptionText: Fusion of synaptic vesicles with the presynaptic membrane

distractorRationale.a: Ca2+ channels are not SNARE proteins.
distractorRationale.b: Receptors are postsynaptic and unaffected by a presynaptic SNARE toxin.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: SNARE proteins mediate vesicle docking and fusion, so cleaving them blocks transmitter release.
distractorRationale.d: The presynaptic spike is not affected.

questions.explanation: SNARE proteins form the complex that pulls vesicle and plasma membranes together for exocytosis. Cleaving them prevents transmitter release even though the nerve conducts normally and Ca2+ enters, which produces flaccid paralysis in botulism.

questions.stem: Explain how a neurone integrates excitatory and inhibitory inputs to decide whether to fire. Include where integration occurs, the difference between spatial and temporal summation, and one way that inhibition opposes excitation.
markingGuide: PSPs are graded, small and decay with time and distance
Integration occurs at the axon initial segment/hillock where Na+ channel density is highest
Spatial summation: PSPs from different synapses arriving at the same time are added
Temporal summation: successive PSPs from one synapse overlap and add
EPSPs depolarise and IPSPs hyperpolarise (or hold near rest), so net potential is compared with threshold
Inhibition opposes excitation by opening Cl- or K+ channels that pull Vm away from threshold
Action potential occurs only if threshold is reached
questions.explanation: Each synapse produces a small graded change; the cell sums them across space and time at the axon hillock. IPSPs subtract from the total, so firing occurs only when the net depolarisation reaches threshold.
